LEADER-AL20-3.1.title: AL20 3.1: public-interest studies and plans
LEADER-AL20-3.1.availability: Selected AL20 typology; applicable call, budget and applicant eligibility require confirmation.
unresolved: Confirm the exact typology, applicant, local call, eligible costs and route-specific selection criteria with AL20.
LEADER-AL20-3.1.what: LEADER is a rural-development programme delivered through local action groups. AL20 is the Alpujarra–Sierra Nevada Almeriense territory. Route 3.1 concerns studies, plans and programmes serving rural conservation, quality of life or sustainable development, with a useful public-interest product rather than ordinary private consultancy.
LEADER-AL20-3.1.fit: Illustrative fit: a competent nonprofit or public partner commissions an ecological baseline and a practical restoration plan for a local area. The output could explain habitat conditions, pressures, suitable methods and how landholders can use the findings. This does not establish applicant or project eligibility.
LEADER-AL20-3.1.advantages: The route can support the knowledge needed before spending on physical interventions. A shared diagnosis or management plan could benefit several parcels and clarify the public purpose of later work. It may suit a project whose most useful first result is evidence rather than construction.
LEADER-AL20-3.1.limitations: The study must fit the exact typology and territorial conditions. Routine grant-writing or a private technical design cannot automatically be relabelled public-interest research. Eligible applicants, costs, procurement and dissemination require checking. Selection scoring is a separate requirement, and this option’s automated assessment is not implemented.
LEADER-AL20-3.1.next_steps: Discuss a defined output and intended users with AL20 before commissioning work. Check the governing rules, local selected activities, current call and aid-line selection criteria. Prepare methods, provider competence, budget and public-use arrangements; compare 3.3 outreach or 3.4 demonstration when those are the actual main activity.

LEADER-AL20-3.3.title: AL20 3.3: information and awareness
LEADER-AL20-3.3.availability: Selected AL20 typology; no award or current application eligibility is established by this guide.
unresolved: Confirm the exact typology, applicant, local call, eligible costs and route-specific selection criteria with AL20.
LEADER-AL20-3.3.what: This local LEADER route concerns eligible promotion, information and awareness activities supporting rural public-benefit objectives. It is distinct from advertising a company’s products. The organiser, audience, content and intended outcomes need to fit the exact legal typology and AL20’s local priorities.
LEADER-AL20-3.3.fit: Illustrative fit: a qualifying organisation develops an accessible local guide to native dryland habitats and runs practical learning events for landholders. An activity could explain erosion observations or natural regeneration using evidence from Algarrobos, with materials available to the intended public.
LEADER-AL20-3.3.advantages: It can make ecological learning useful beyond the pilot parcel and support relationships with schools, residents and practitioners. Communication has value in its own right when it improves understanding and participation. A focused outreach programme may be a better match than trying to classify every event as an experiment.
LEADER-AL20-3.3.limitations: Ordinary commercial marketing, recurring activities without the required added value or capital works may not fit. Applicant status, eligible expenses, permissions and public-benefit conditions need checking. A worthwhile event still needs the applicable selection assessment. This node currently explains the route without calculating eligibility or support.
LEADER-AL20-3.3.next_steps: Define the audience, learning outcomes, programme, access and evidence of participation. Ask AL20 to confirm classification and current call conditions before commitments. Check the local scoring profile and budget rules. Use 3.1 for a genuine study and 3.4 for an actual novel demonstration rather than choosing by a preferred grant ceiling.

LEADER-AL20-3.6.title: AL20 3.6: public-benefit facilities and services
LEADER-AL20-3.6.availability: Selected AL20 typology; project classification and current call conditions need AL20 verification.
unresolved: Confirm the exact typology, applicant, local call, eligible costs and route-specific selection criteria with AL20.
LEADER-AL20-3.6.what: This LEADER category concerns eligible infrastructure, equipment, tools or services supporting sustainable rural public benefit. It has its own boundaries and is not a general green-project fund. The primary purpose must match the category rather than a productive business investment or another specifically defined activity.
LEADER-AL20-3.6.fit: Illustrative fit: a qualifying public or nonprofit body explores a shared nature-learning resource or community monitoring facility with real users and an operating plan. Algarrobos could contribute experience, but a proprietary software product or a private equipment collection would need a different assessment.
LEADER-AL20-3.6.advantages: The route may help create a durable service that several people or organisations can use. It encourages attention to access, operation and maintenance, rather than only initial installation. An institutional partner can connect the facility with an actual local need and continuing responsibility.
LEADER-AL20-3.6.limitations: The rules distinguish this category from studies, outreach, demonstrations and heritage restoration covered elsewhere. Applicant qualification, nonproductive purpose, permissions and eligible costs remain essential. A building or tool described as environmental is not automatically eligible. The current explorer does not calculate this route’s eligibility or selection score.
LEADER-AL20-3.6.next_steps: Write down the service, beneficiaries, location, access and whole-life operating costs. Seek AL20 classification before design or purchasing commitments. Review the exact typology and local selection criteria, and compare 3.1, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 so the proposal follows its actual principal purpose.

LEADER-AL20-1.7.title: AL20 1.7: investment in genuine farms
LEADER-AL20-1.7.availability: Selected productive-investment category; no farm, parcel or investment eligibility is assumed.
unresolved: Confirm the exact typology, applicant, local call, eligible costs and route-specific selection criteria with AL20.
LEADER-AL20-1.7.what: This LEADER route supports qualifying start-up, modernisation or competitiveness investments in agricultural holdings. It concerns genuine farming operations, not every parcel containing trees. Farm status, investment purpose and the applicable applicant conditions determine whether the category is relevant.
LEADER-AL20-1.7.fit: Illustrative fit: a legitimate rain-fed farm investigates an eligible investment that improves operations while protecting soil and valuable habitat. A carob-related activity might be considered only where it is a real agricultural business. Algarrobos’ ecological restoration objectives alone do not turn shrubland into a farm.
LEADER-AL20-1.7.advantages: The route can connect environmental improvements with an existing productive operation and a viable business plan. A farmer partner may bring practical experience, equipment and continuity. It offers a more specific starting point for agricultural investment than broad nature-finance mechanisms without an identified provider.
LEADER-AL20-1.7.limitations: Registration, economic purpose, investment eligibility, permissions and start conditions need checking. Irrigation-related restrictions require particular care; water access cannot be assumed. Own finance and reimbursement timing may matter. EU-PRIMA.fit: Illustrative fit: a research partnership tests ecologically defensible dryland soil-water management with actual agricultural users. Algarrobos might contribute observations or a pilot where its setting answers the topic’s question. A nature reserve without a relevant research or farming connection may be a weak fit.
EU-PRIMA.advantages: The Mediterranean focus can connect the project with similar climatic constraints and applied research partners. Collaboration may help link technical tools with real land-management decisions. A defined field contribution can be useful without asking a small initiative to coordinate the full international proposal.
EU-PRIMA.limitations: Eligible countries, partner types, topic scope, funding section and national conditions must be checked. General water scarcity is not enough to fit a specialised topic such as desalination. The official work-programme PDF download was blocked during this research, so it is retained as a lead rather than a locally inspected document.
EU-PRIMA.next_steps: Read the precise topic and obtain the complete work programme and applicant guidance from PRIMA before committing. Confirm the funding agency for each partner, scientific roles and costs. Compare Operational Groups or Soil Mission topics if they better match the actual research problem and practical users.

EU-ERASMUS-EDUCATION.title: Erasmus+ education and vocational partnerships
EU-ERASMUS-EDUCATION.availability: Action-specific calls and deadlines apply; no currently open education grant is confirmed here.
unresolved: Confirm a precise current instrument, applicant/partner role, territorial fit, costs and timetable before treating this as project funding.
EU-ERASMUS-EDUCATION.what: Erasmus+ supports education, training, youth and cooperation through distinct actions. A partnership grant concerns learning and organisational cooperation, not simply environmental expenditure. The programme guide and relevant national or European call determine who can coordinate, participate and receive support.
EU-ERASMUS-EDUCATION.fit: Illustrative fit: experienced education partners develop practical training materials on dryland habitat observations or ecological field skills. Algarrobos could host suitable learning activities or contribute evidence, provided the project serves defined learners and the action permits the proposed role and costs.
EU-ERASMUS-EDUCATION.advantages: The programme can connect practical experience with teaching expertise and international exchange. Environmental work becomes a learning setting rather than an isolated site activity. A smaller organisation may find a proportionate partnership role while building the competence needed for future training or community projects.
EU-ERASMUS-EDUCATION.limitations: Learning objectives, eligible organisations, partnership composition, coordinator experience and participant safeguards matter. A training label cannot turn a land-purchase or planting budget into an education project. Different actions have different grant formats and deadlines, and a general environmental priority does not establish eligibility.
EU-ERASMUS-EDUCATION.next_steps: Choose the intended learners and outcomes first, then select the precise action and current guide. Consult the relevant national agency or experienced lead organisation about a realistic role. Define curriculum, access, safety, evaluation and costs, and compare Empleaverde+ where employment outcomes rather than educational cooperation are the main purpose.

EU-CERV-SOLIDARITY.title: Civic participation and European volunteering
EU-CERV-SOLIDARITY.availability: CERV and the European Solidarity Corps are separate programmes; each requires its own eligible action and timetable.
unresolved: Confirm a precise current instrument, applicant/partner role, territorial fit, costs and timetable before treating this as project funding.
EU-CERV-SOLIDARITY.what: This catalogue node groups two different avenues for community participation. CERV means Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values and concerns civic and democratic objectives. The European Solidarity Corps supports eligible solidarity and volunteering activities. Their rules, participants and application processes must be considered separately.
EU-CERV-SOLIDARITY.fit: Illustrative fit: a competent organisation develops an inclusive community-learning or environmental-volunteering project with a genuine social purpose. Algarrobos could provide a suitable setting or practical contribution. The activity must serve the selected programme’s objectives, rather than using volunteers only to reduce restoration labour costs.
EU-CERV-SOLIDARITY.advantages: These routes can build participation, skills and relationships around conservation. An experienced organisation may provide safeguarding and volunteer support that a small site cannot offer alone. Community outcomes can be valuable even when physical habitat work is a limited part of the project.
EU-CERV-SOLIDARITY.limitations: Programme-specific eligibility, participant ages or target groups, accreditation, supervision and reporting may apply. Volunteer support is not unrestricted cash for landowners, and civic participation funding is not a general forestry grant. Young or vulnerable participants need appropriate arrangements. No current local intake or award is assumed.
EU-CERV-SOLIDARITY.next_steps: Decide whether the central objective is civic participation or solidarity volunteering before choosing the programme. Consult its official guide and national contact point, then define learning, inclusion, safety and staff capacity. Work through an experienced host if appropriate and keep donated time separate from cash and eligible grant expenditure.

EU-INNOVATION-SME.title: European innovation support for real ventures
EU-INNOVATION-SME.availability: A family of competitive innovation instruments; the exact programme, funding type and current intake must be identified.
unresolved: Confirm a precise current instrument, applicant/partner role, territorial fit, costs and timetable before treating this as project funding.
EU-INNOVATION-SME.what: European innovation support includes programmes and accelerators for ventures developing genuinely innovative products or technologies. EIC is the European Innovation Council; EIT communities offer other opportunities with their own rules. Grants, investment, advice and training are different instruments and must not be treated as equivalent cash awards.
EU-INNOVATION-SME.fit: Illustrative fit: a capable venture validates a technically novel monitoring product with identified customers and wider market potential. Algarrobos might supply a test setting, but a general website or local planting activity would not establish the innovation and commercial case expected by technology-focused programmes.
EU-INNOVATION-SME.advantages: A suitable programme can connect development finance with specialist advice, partners and customers. It may help a team turn a useful prototype into a business serving many projects. Support for product development can complement field learning when the venture solves a real problem beyond the pilot site.
EU-INNOVATION-SME.limitations: Technology maturity, novelty, intellectual property, legal form, commercial potential and team capacity are decisive. Competition and preparation can be substantial. Some schemes provide services rather than cash, and investment can involve ownership or repayment obligations. A project’s environmental purpose alone does not satisfy deep-technology criteria.
EU-INNOVATION-SME.next_steps: Identify the product, customer problem and evidence of technical advantage, then choose a named instrument. Read its current terms and confirm whether support is a grant, service or investment. Build a realistic development and market plan, and compare ordinary paid data services when innovation funding is not the appropriate route.

ES-CDTI-ENISA-TECH.title: Spanish innovation finance: CDTI and ENISA
ES-CDTI-ENISA-TECH.availability: Different instruments with current terms to verify; ENISA participative loans are repayable and do not confer equity ownership.
unresolved: Confirm a precise current instrument, applicant/partner role, territorial fit, costs and timetable before treating this as project funding.
ES-CDTI-ENISA-TECH.what: CDTI and ENISA provide different kinds of support for eligible innovative businesses in Spain. CDTI instruments can concern research and technological development; ENISA uses participative loans under its financing arrangements. A participative loan remains debt even when part of its interest relates to business performance.
ES-CDTI-ENISA-TECH.fit: Illustrative fit: a viable Spanish company develops a validated environmental-monitoring product or technical service with a credible market. Algarrobos could help test practical needs. A nonprofit habitat pilot with no commercial repayment model should not assume it qualifies merely because it uses software or sensors.
ES-CDTI-ENISA-TECH.advantages: A well-matched instrument may support development and growth while connecting the venture with business or technical expertise. ENISA’s financing differs from selling shares, while CDTI opportunities may fit defined research work. Understanding those differences helps choose finance that matches the venture’s actual stage.
ES-CDTI-ENISA-TECH.limitations: Legal form, innovation, own resources, financial capacity, eligible costs and repayment terms vary by instrument. Older line names and third-party summaries can be outdated. A public lender is not a charitable donor, and loan approval is not guaranteed. Ordinary digital implementation may not qualify as research and development.
ES-CDTI-ENISA-TECH.next_steps: Start with the business, product, customers and capital requirement. Check the current provider guidance, including cofinancing and full borrowing cost, then obtain appropriate financial advice. Keep grant, loan and equity amounts separate. Compare European innovation support without counting the same development cost or finance twice.

EU-GREEN-ASSIST-ADVISORY.title: Green Assist investment-readiness advice
EU-GREEN-ASSIST-ADVISORY.availability: The October 2026 water accelerator requested approaches by end October; that date has passed and any extension or later intake is unverified.
unresolved: Confirm a precise current instrument, applicant/partner role, territorial fit, costs and timetable before treating this as project funding.
EU-GREEN-ASSIST-ADVISORY.what: Green Assist provides advisory support intended to help eligible environmental projects become ready for investment. The Water Resilience Investment Accelerator announced in October 2026 is a related targeted initiative. Advice may address project development and financing, rather than paying for implementation works or land purchase.
EU-GREEN-ASSIST-ADVISORY.fit: Illustrative fit: a sufficiently developed water-resilience project needs help structuring a realistic investment case and identifying appropriate finance. Algarrobos might participate within a larger eligible partnership. A small exploratory parcel with no investment model may be too early or outside the particular advisory initiative’s focus.
EU-GREEN-ASSIST-ADVISORY.advantages: Specialist advice can help resolve financial and organisational questions before a project accepts major obligations. A useful review might reveal a simpler funding structure or identify missing evidence. Access to expertise can be valuable even where the support does not create a direct cash contribution.
EU-GREEN-ASSIST-ADVISORY.limitations: The initiative has its own selection, scale and intake conditions. Advisory support is not an investment approval, lender commitment or grant award. The announcement’s end-October approach date has passed as of this guide. Environmental relevance alone does not establish that the project is ready or eligible for the service.
EU-GREEN-ASSIST-ADVISORY.next_steps: Check the latest official guidance for an extension or future intake before preparing an application. Describe the actual investment, development stage, financing problem and intended outcomes. Confirm what advice would be delivered and by whom, then record it as support rather than spendable funds or an assumed implementation budget.

NATURE-01.title: Payments for ecosystem services
NATURE-01.availability: Requires an identifiable beneficiary and negotiated payment agreement; there is no standard public tariff.
unresolved: Who will pay for which locally relevant service and on what evidence?
NATURE-01.what: A beneficiary of an ecosystem service pays a landholder or manager to maintain or improve it. The service could concern soil retention, water quality or habitat management. A direct agreement can define activities and payments without creating a tradable environmental certificate.
NATURE-01.fit: Illustrative fit: downstream stakeholders help finance agreed erosion-management work and independent observations across suitable parcels. The project would need to show why those stakeholders benefit and what the management can reasonably achieve. Increased surface infiltration alone would not establish additional groundwater recharge.
NATURE-01.advantages: Payments can connect conservation with people who depend on the landscape and could support repeated management rather than a single installation. A local agreement may be more practical than building a certified credit project, particularly when the service and beneficiary are readily identifiable.
NATURE-01.limitations: Finding a willing payer is often the central obstacle. Service measurement, land rights, rainfall variation and attribution can make agreements costly. The contract must define whether payment depends on actions or measured outcomes, who bears failure risk and whether other funding or claims overlap.
NATURE-01.next_steps: Identify a real beneficiary and discuss the problem before designing a payment unit. Agree the baseline, service boundary, management, monitoring, price and duration. Seek appropriate technical and legal review. Compare results-based contracts and voluntary contributions, then record the actual agreement only once.

NATURE-02.title: Payments for verified restoration results
NATURE-02.availability: A payer and an agreed outcome contract must exist; ecological improvement alone creates no receivable.
unresolved: Who verifies results and carries weather, delay and partial-success risk?
NATURE-02.what: A funder pays against specified restoration results rather than simply reimbursing activities. Milestones could concern habitat condition, plant establishment or another defensible indicator. The contract determines how results are measured, verified and translated into payments, including any minimum or partial payment.
NATURE-02.fit: Illustrative fit: a foundation finances repeated assessments of native cover and erosion across a plot network, releasing payments when agreed, independently checked milestones are met. Indicators should suit the reference habitat, rather than rewarding tree density where natural shrubland is the desired outcome.
NATURE-02.advantages: The approach can align finance with ecological performance and encourage learning about methods that work. It may give managers flexibility over techniques. A well-designed agreement can support longer observation periods and make the purpose of monitoring understandable to both payer and landholder.
NATURE-02.limitations: Results can take years and depend on weather or pressures outside the manager’s control. Monitoring and verification may cost too much for a tiny site. Poor baselines or narrow indicators can reward misleading improvements. The manager may need cash before any performance payment is due.
NATURE-02.next_steps: Find the payer, choose a defensible baseline and test the proposed indicators. Agree who verifies results, how drought and delays are handled, and how disputes or partial success affect payment. Compare a simpler activity-based stewardship contract when ecological uncertainty cannot be shared fairly.

NATURE-03.title: Digital memberships linked to conservation results
NATURE-03.availability: Requires recurring supporters and an affordable reporting service; it is not a certified credit scheme.
unresolved: Can recurring income cover the promised digital reporting and fieldwork?
NATURE-03.what: Supporters make recurring contributions and receive regular information about conservation work, often through a website or digital membership platform. The connection with results is a reporting commitment, not automatically a promise of ownership, investment return or a quantified environmental credit.
NATURE-03.fit: Illustrative fit: supporters follow seasonal observations from Algarrobos through short reports, photographs and clearly explained indicators. A membership could help pay for repeat field visits while showing both progress and setbacks, including drought impacts or a decision to favour natural regeneration over planting.
NATURE-03.advantages: The scheme can make long-term work visible and build continuity between campaigns. Digital communication lets distant supporters stay involved. Recurring contributions may support coordination and monitoring that do not fit neatly into a one-off appeal for equipment or plants.
NATURE-03.limitations: Reporting, technology, customer support and payment administration have real costs. Subscribers can leave, and unclear benefits may create commercial or consumer obligations. A dashboard must not imply independent certification it does not have. Paid membership must not restrict participation that another funder requires to be open.
NATURE-03.next_steps: Define the relationship, reporting frequency, cancellation rules and expected running costs. Explain which indicators are observations and which are independently verified. Start with a manageable supporter group. Compare ordinary nonprofit membership and donation crowdfunding so the same recurring contribution is not counted twice.

NATURE-04.title: Environmental compensation arrangements
NATURE-04.availability: Only a legally and ecologically valid compensation arrangement creates an opportunity; no obligation or buyer is assumed.
unresolved: What approved obligation, equivalence and mitigation hierarchy apply?
NATURE-04.what: A developer or other responsible party finances measures connected with an environmental impact under a specific legal or voluntary arrangement. Compensation is different from a general gift: it concerns a defined loss, an assessment process and conditions on what can count toward addressing that loss.
NATURE-04.fit: Illustrative fit: an authorised restoration site could be considered within a properly designed compensation plan if its habitat, location, timing and management satisfy the applicable requirements. Algarrobos should first ask whether the ecological outcome is appropriate, rather than assuming any planting can replace damage elsewhere.
NATURE-04.advantages: Where a legitimate arrangement exists, it may bring resources for long-term management and monitoring. Clear obligations can make responsibilities more explicit than an informal donation. It can also connect land managers with technical teams that must document actual environmental outcomes.
NATURE-04.limitations: Avoidance and reduction of harm come before compensation. Some losses cannot be replaced, and no generic hectare-for-hectare exchange is assumed. Equivalence, additionality, permanence and legal approval are difficult questions. Reputational risk arises if a conservation project helps justify damaging development without a defensible basis.
NATURE-04.next_steps: Identify the actual obligation and competent authority. Obtain the approved ecological rationale, management responsibilities and verification requirements before negotiating. Distinguish statutory compensation from voluntary contribution claims, and check for duplicate claims against public grants or credits already associated with the same outcomes.

NATURE-05.title: Environmental insurance arrangements
NATURE-05.availability: Requires a suitable insurance product and accepted policy; protection does not itself finance restoration activities.
unresolved: Which actual policy covers the disclosed risks and exclusions?
NATURE-05.what: Insurance transfers specified risks to an insurer in exchange for a premium. Environmental cover may concern defined liabilities, damage or recovery costs. The policy wording, exclusions, insured party and claims process determine the protection; the environmental label does not make all ecological losses insurable.
NATURE-05.fit: Illustrative fit: an organisation investigates liability cover for authorised public activities or a contractor reviews insurance for work on another owner’s land. A specialist policy might help address a particular restoration exposure, but availability must be confirmed with an insurer for the actual project.
NATURE-05.advantages: Appropriate cover can protect organisational continuity and reassure partners or clients. It may make a land-use agreement or contract feasible where a party otherwise cannot accept the risk. Examining cover also helps identify responsibilities that need clearer allocation before work starts.
NATURE-05.limitations: Premiums, deductibles, exclusions, limits and proof requirements can leave substantial exposure. Gradual ecological change, drought or failure to achieve an ambitious habitat target may not be covered. Insurance is a cost and contingent protection, rather than unrestricted income or a guarantee that restoration will succeed.
NATURE-05.next_steps: List actual liabilities and operational risks, then request policy wording and a written explanation of relevant exclusions. Confirm land access, public activity and contractor arrangements are accurately disclosed. Compare insurance with contractual guarantees and reserves, and budget premiums without counting hypothetical claim payments as available funding.

NATURE-06.title: Biodiversity and nature credits
NATURE-06.availability: Emerging, method- and buyer-dependent; the EU roadmap is not a grant or a universal approved unit.
unresolved: Which method, verifier and buyer accept this habitat and its claimed outcomes?
NATURE-06.what: A nature-credit arrangement aims to finance independently documented benefits for biodiversity through units defined by a particular method. A baseline, management actions, verification and buyer agreement are needed. The European Commission’s July 2025 roadmap describes development of this market, rather than an automatic payment system.
NATURE-06.fit: Illustrative fit: a network of suitable restoration sites investigates whether a credible standard recognises its habitat improvements. Algarrobos could contribute field evidence and management experience. Existing native scrub must be evaluated on its own ecological merits; planting more trees is not automatically a biodiversity gain.
NATURE-06.advantages: The idea could connect long-term conservation with private buyers seeking evidenced contributions to nature. Shared monitoring or aggregation might make smaller sites more practical. Exploring requirements can also clarify which baseline observations and management commitments are valuable even if no credit is ultimately sold.
NATURE-06.limitations: Methods, units, buyer demand and allowable claims vary. Certification and monitoring costs may exceed revenue. Additionality, land rights, permanence and double counting require scrutiny. A contribution to nature differs from compensating for a company’s impacts, and no guaranteed price or hectare-to-credit conversion is assumed.
NATURE-06.next_steps: Identify the actual standard, verifier and prospective buyer before forecasting income. Examine eligibility, claim ownership, fees and long-term obligations. Compare a simpler donation or ecosystem-service agreement, and document unresolved methodological questions rather than representing an early market concept as secured finance.

NATURE-07.title: Voluntary carbon-market credits
NATURE-07.availability: Requires an applicable standard, verified units and a buyer; separate registry systems have different rules.
unresolved: Which standard applies and who owns issued units and reversal liabilities?
NATURE-07.what: A carbon project quantifies additional climate benefits under a specified method, obtains the required validation or verification and sells eligible units. Standards differ in eligible activities, accounting, timing and permitted claims. A planted tree or modelled carbon estimate is not by itself a saleable credit.
NATURE-07.fit: Illustrative fit: a suitable group of landholders investigates a recognised method for ecologically appropriate forest establishment or management. The project would need evidence of past land use, future management and climate risks. A small demonstration could improve knowledge without qualifying as an independent credit project.
NATURE-07.advantages: A genuine buyer agreement can potentially link long-term management with financial support. Aggregating sites may help share specialist costs. The method’s evidence requirements can encourage careful baseline records, although monitoring has value even when commercial certification proves impractical.
NATURE-07.limitations: Additionality, permanence, fire, drought, leakage, verification costs and ownership of claims are material constraints. Spain’s national forest-absorption registry is distinct from voluntary standards and EU certification frameworks. Its minimum-area and duration requirements cannot be ignored or silently borrowed for another standard. No future credit price is assumed.
NATURE-07.next_steps: Choose the actual registry and method, test eligibility and obtain a full cost estimate before choosing a planting design. Clarify who owns the units and carries reversal risk. Confirm interactions with grants and other claims, then distinguish expected issuance from contracted sales and cash received.

NATURE-08.title: Water-benefit credits
NATURE-08.availability: Emerging and often bespoke; no universal Spanish water-credit tariff or automatic certificate is assumed.
unresolved: What water outcome, basin boundary and beneficiary can be independently demonstrated?
NATURE-08.what: A water-benefit arrangement attempts to quantify and finance a specified improvement in water quantity, quality or catchment function. Some programmes describe these benefits as credits. The method and buyer determine whether a unit exists and what claim it supports; different water outcomes cannot be treated as interchangeable.
NATURE-08.fit: Illustrative fit: a catchment partnership tests whether erosion management reduces sediment pressure relevant to a particular water user. Another project might examine demand reduction or retention. Algarrobos would need hydrological expertise to establish whether a site-level measure benefits the intended basin and time period.
NATURE-08.advantages: The approach can direct attention to businesses or communities with a real interest in water resilience. A credible agreement may finance monitoring and maintenance as well as initial works. Catchment collaboration can connect small sites to a more meaningful scale of evidence.
NATURE-08.limitations: Infiltration does not automatically equal additional aquifer recharge. Rainfall, evaporation, displaced water use and legal rights complicate attribution. Verification may be expensive and buyers scarce. A water-saving claim in one basin does not automatically compensate for withdrawals in another, and the same benefit cannot be sold repeatedly.
NATURE-08.next_steps: Define the water outcome and beneficiary before discussing credits. Review water rights, baseline, catchment boundaries, timing and independent verification. Obtain buyer terms and compare a direct ecosystem-service agreement, which may achieve the purpose without a tradable unit or costly certification infrastructure.

NATURE-09.title: Environmental investment funds
NATURE-09.availability: Requires a fund willing to invest in a financially viable project or portfolio.
unresolved: Does a real fund’s mandate and transaction size match a viable revenue model?
NATURE-09.what: An environmental investment fund pools capital and invests in assets or businesses expected to generate financial returns alongside environmental objectives. It may provide debt, equity or a combination. The fund’s mandate determines eligible sectors, geography, transaction size, return expectations and investment period.
NATURE-09.fit: Illustrative fit: a portfolio of conservation-compatible land-management businesses has reliable service or product revenues and seeks expansion capital. A small Algarrobos pilot could supply evidence or join a wider partnership, while a site managed solely for public benefit may have no investment repayment model.
NATURE-09.advantages: Funds can mobilise more capital than a small local fundraising campaign and may bring financial structuring expertise. A portfolio can spread some project costs across multiple sites. An appropriately matched investor might support operations and management systems beyond initial establishment.
NATURE-09.limitations: The project must generate returns and satisfy due diligence. Minimum transaction sizes can exclude small initiatives. Control of assets, investor exit and pressure for commercial use may conflict with conservation permanence. A fund described as green is not automatically a philanthropic donor or an accessible open application.
NATURE-09.next_steps: Identify an actual fund and read its mandate before preparing a pitch. Establish the legal vehicle, revenue contracts, capital need and conservation protections. Clarify ownership, reporting and exit terms. Compare impact equity and green lending as alternative descriptions of the same financing transaction.

NATURE-10.title: Impact investment funds
NATURE-10.availability: Return-seeking capital; suitability depends on a real business and the fund’s mandate.
unresolved: Can the venture demonstrate both financial returns and attributable impact?
NATURE-10.what: Impact investors seek both a financial return and intentional, measurable social or environmental benefits. Funding may be equity or debt, with reporting tied to the investor’s objectives. Demonstrating a worthwhile ecological purpose is necessary context but does not replace a credible business model.
NATURE-10.fit: Illustrative fit: an ecological monitoring service or restoration contractor grows through paying customers and can show how its work improves practice. Algarrobos could be a test site or customer reference. A donation-funded land reserve would need a different structure if it cannot generate investor returns.
NATURE-10.advantages: A well-matched investor can combine capital with commercial advice, networks and attention to impact measurement. This may suit a venture whose value emerges over several years. Explicit impact objectives can help negotiate safeguards that a purely financial investor might otherwise overlook.
NATURE-10.limitations: Measurement and financial reporting take staff time. Investor definitions of impact may differ from ecological priorities. Growth targets, ownership rights and exit requirements can affect decisions about habitat and public benefit. Capital is neither free nor guaranteed, and the label does not ensure patient or concessionary terms.
NATURE-10.next_steps: Prepare evidence of customers, financial viability and attributable environmental outcomes. Examine the fund’s track record and actual investment terms. Agree governance and conservation safeguards before accepting capital, and compare ordinary equity or debt to understand whether the impact arrangement changes the obligations in a useful way.

NATURE-11.title: Certified products supporting stewardship
NATURE-11.availability: Requires lawful production, an applicable assurance scheme and customers; premiums are not guaranteed.
unresolved: Does certification improve real sales enough to cover compliance costs?
NATURE-11.what: A producer sells goods whose origin or management meets a named certification or assurance standard. Certification may help buyers recognise a particular attribute, but the sale remains a commercial transaction. Different labels address different features and do not all establish ecological restoration or biodiversity gain.
NATURE-11.fit: Illustrative fit: a legitimate farm sells qualifying products while maintaining conservation areas, or a nursery documents the origin and quality of native stock. A stewardship story can help explain responsible management, provided the product and its claims genuinely meet the relevant requirements.
NATURE-11.advantages: Sales can connect continued management with customers and provide revenue beyond a grant period. Credible traceability may distinguish a product in a suitable market. Partnerships with existing producers could be more practical than starting a new processing or distribution business around a small pilot.
NATURE-11.limitations: Certification, audits, processing and marketing cost money. Demand and price premiums remain uncertain. Harvest rights, plant health, provenance and ecological suitability must be checked. Certification for farming practices is not a carbon or biodiversity credit, and valuable natural scrub should not be removed to invent a product stream.
NATURE-11.next_steps: Identify the product, lawful supply and buyer first. Compare certification requirements and costs with realistic sales margins. Document conservation claims and agree how proceeds support stewardship. Assess drought and yield delays, and avoid counting the same product income again under the general production node.

NATURE-12.title: Voluntary contributions from local beneficiaries
NATURE-12.availability: Requires willing contributors; it does not assume a statutory levy, credit buyer or public award.
unresolved: Which beneficiaries are willing to contribute and what do they receive?
NATURE-12.what: People or businesses that benefit from a healthy landscape contribute voluntarily toward its care. They might value reduced erosion, attractive surroundings or community access. The contribution can be a donation, cost-sharing agreement or contract, depending on what the payer receives and how responsibilities are defined.
NATURE-12.fit: Illustrative fit: nearby landowners and tourism businesses jointly support observations and conservation-compatible management around a shared landscape. The project could begin with a modest agreed activity and transparent spending, without claiming that every contributor has purchased a measurable offset.
NATURE-12.advantages: This can work through existing local relationships and a benefit people understand. A straightforward contribution may be more proportionate than certified environmental units. Pooling small commitments can share coordination costs and build a constituency for maintaining the site over time.
NATURE-12.limitations: Benefits may be diffuse, so people can decline to pay while still benefiting. Informal expectations can create disagreements about access, influence and publicity. Contributions need appropriate accounting, and a voluntary arrangement cannot be represented as an enforceable public tax or guaranteed long-term income.
NATURE-12.next_steps: Talk with actual beneficiaries about the problem and affordable commitments. Define whether support is a gift, sponsorship or payment for services. Agree responsibilities, reporting and permitted claims in writing. Compare ecosystem-service payments when the benefit and performance obligations are specific enough to support a formal contract.

NATURE-13.title: Community assets contributed to conservation
NATURE-13.availability: An enabling asset or right, not automatically cash; legal transferability must be established.
unresolved: Can the asset be lawfully transferred and maintained without creating a cash shortfall?
NATURE-13.what: Land, buildings, equipment or usable rights can be contributed to strengthen a community conservation initiative. A transfer may be permanent or time-limited and can carry restrictions. The asset’s practical value depends on whether the recipient can lawfully use, maintain and, where relevant, transfer it.
NATURE-13.fit: Illustrative fit: an owner provides storage space for monitoring equipment, a suitable parcel is donated, or a municipality considers authorised use of a public facility. These different arrangements need their own legal procedures and should not all be represented as unrestricted financial contributions.
NATURE-13.advantages: Useful assets can remove practical barriers that a cash-only budget misses. Long-term access or equipment may allow a project to begin with fewer purchases. Community ownership can also support participation and continuity when the organisation has a realistic operating and maintenance plan.
NATURE-13.limitations: Title, encumbrances, public-property rules, taxes, liability and operating costs can outweigh the benefit. Donated land cannot pay a supplier’s invoice. A public authority may lack power to transfer an asset informally, and restrictions may prevent the use proposed by the conservation project.
NATURE-13.next_steps: List the actual rights and condition of the asset, identify the authorised owner and cost its upkeep. Obtain an appropriate written agreement and confirm any valuation or grant-matching rules. Record the asset separately from cash and compare land donation, leases and public-land arrangements for the specific transaction.

NATURE-14.title: Income from nature visits and learning
NATURE-14.availability: Requires lawful access, suitable activities and paying customers; sensitive habitat may limit use.
unresolved: Are access, professional requirements, demand and ecological visitor capacity suitable?
NATURE-14.what: A provider earns income from guided visits, interpretation, courses or other nature-related experiences. The customer pays for a service, rather than donating without a return. Cultural or wellbeing themes can be part of an activity, but medical claims require appropriate evidence and qualifications.
NATURE-14.fit: Illustrative fit: a qualified guide runs a small dryland ecology walk, or an instructor teaches repeatable field observations at an authorised site. Algarrobos could explain how restoration decisions are made while limiting visitor numbers and keeping fragile areas outside the activity.
NATURE-14.advantages: Activities can connect education, local engagement and revenue. Small events can test customer interest before investing in facilities. They may also improve the public understanding and practical skills that support conservation, while providing a clear service rather than a vague promise of environmental benefit.
NATURE-14.limitations: Demand, travel, weather, staffing, insurance and permits affect profitability. Public access and commercial use may conflict with land agreements or nonproductive grant conditions. Repeated visits can disturb wildlife or vegetation. A conservation benefit does not remove the need for proper cancellation and consumer terms.
NATURE-14.next_steps: Define the audience, learning purpose, safe capacity and delivery costs. Confirm land permissions and applicable professional requirements. Test an accessible, low-impact activity and collect feedback. Keep its commercial income distinct from donations or public education grants, and check compatibility before selling access to a funded site.

NATURE-15.title: Philanthropy and environmental crowdfunding
NATURE-15.availability: A broad family of voluntary giving routes, not an additional pot alongside their individual nodes.
unresolved: Which specific giving routes and recipient arrangements are feasible?
NATURE-15.what: Philanthropy includes individual donations, foundation grants, major gifts and other voluntary support for public benefit. Environmental crowdfunding brings many such contributions together. This node describes the wider fundraising approach; the catalogue’s donation, foundation and campaign nodes explain more specific ways to organise it.
NATURE-15.fit: Illustrative fit: an established nonprofit combines a foundation grant for baseline surveys with public donations for equipment and unrestricted support for coordination. A land gift might contribute separately. Each source would need its own terms and accounting rather than a single assumed philanthropic entitlement.
NATURE-15.advantages: Giving can support activities that have clear public value but no commercial repayment model. Donor relationships may provide continuity and flexibility. A credible organisation can use evidence and transparent reporting to connect people with conservation outcomes over several seasons.
NATURE-15.limitations: Raising money costs time and income can fluctuate. Restrictions, donor influence and public claims must be managed. Spanish charitable tax treatment depends on recipient qualification and the actual gift; a newly registered association does not automatically inherit every incentive. A hosting organisation legally receives and controls funds under the agreed arrangement.
NATURE-15.next_steps: Choose the receiving body and a realistic mix of fundraising methods. Agree governance, restricted budgets, fees, asset ownership and reporting with any host. Build maintenance into appeals and distinguish pledged from received funds. Do not count this umbrella node in addition to the specific gifts it describes.

NATURE-16.title: Voluntary environmental add-ons to purchases
NATURE-16.availability: Requires participating businesses and informed customer consent; it is not a public tax or environmental credit.
unresolved: How will customer consent, transfers, costs and permitted claims be documented?
NATURE-16.what: A business offers customers an optional contribution alongside a booking, product or service. Proceeds support a defined conservation purpose under an agreement with the recipient. The arrangement must explain whether the customer makes a donation or buys something, and how collected money reaches the project.
NATURE-16.fit: Illustrative fit: a local accommodation provider invites guests to add a small voluntary amount for a nonprofit’s habitat monitoring programme. The project publishes periodic spending and activity reports. The payment should not be described as offsetting the guest’s trip unless a separate, defensible system supports that claim.
NATURE-16.advantages: This connects fundraising with an existing customer relationship and can gather many small contributions. It may make local conservation visible to visitors. A participating business can help with communication and collection, reducing the need for the project to build a separate sales channel.
NATURE-16.limitations: Consent, tax treatment, platform fees, refunds and reconciliation need attention. Hidden or preselected charges can damage trust. Collection does not guarantee sustained income, and the business may stop participating. An add-on cannot be represented as a mandatory municipal levy without the relevant legal authority.
NATURE-16.next_steps: Agree the purpose, wording, collection process, transfer schedule and treatment of costs. Explain the voluntary nature clearly and provide evidence of receipts and spending. Confirm permitted claims and compare ordinary corporate sponsorship where the business itself, rather than its customers, is the actual funder.

NATURE-17.title: Climate-resilience outcome credits
NATURE-17.availability: Emerging and highly method-dependent; no standard tradable resilience unit or buyer is established here.
unresolved: Does an accepted resilience method and actual paying counterparty exist?
NATURE-17.what: Some proposed financing arrangements reward independently demonstrated reductions in climate-related risk. The benefit might concern erosion, flood exposure or resilience of an ecosystem. Calling it a credit requires a method that defines a unit and a buyer who accepts the associated claim.
NATURE-17.fit: Illustrative fit: a catchment partnership investigates whether nature-based measures reduce a defined erosion risk for an exposed beneficiary. Algarrobos might contribute monitoring or a pilot site, while technical specialists establish the counterfactual and distinguish the project’s effects from weather and other changes.
NATURE-17.advantages: The idea focuses attention on the practical value of risk reduction and the organisations that benefit from it. It could support longer-term observation and connect conservation with adaptation finance. Testing the logic may help prepare a more conventional resilience project even if no credit market is suitable.
NATURE-17.limitations: Risk is difficult to attribute and avoided losses may never be observed directly. Models, verification and legal claims can be costly. Scenario outputs in this simulator are not market certificates. A buyer, unit, baseline, time horizon and responsibility for failure cannot be assumed from the general concept.
NATURE-17.next_steps: Identify an actual programme or counterparty and ask what evidence it accepts. Compare the cost of the proposed method with likely payments. Consider a direct results-based or ecosystem-service contract, where risk-sharing and verification can be negotiated without creating a supposedly universal tradable unit.

NATURE-18.title: Ecological guarantees and financial security
NATURE-18.availability: A risk-management arrangement; it can tie up cash or require fees rather than create new funding.
unresolved: Which enforceable trigger, security cost and release conditions apply?
NATURE-18.what: A guarantee, reserve or other security arrangement provides assurance that money or remedial action will be available if specified obligations fail. It is linked to a particular contract or risk. The trigger, provider, beneficiary and enforceable wording determine what protection actually exists.
NATURE-18.fit: Illustrative fit: a restoration contract requires security for completion or maintenance, or a funder asks how a long-term commitment will survive organisational difficulties. Algarrobos might investigate a proportionate reserve or guarantee as part of a real agreement, rather than seeking it as an independent grant.
NATURE-18.advantages: Suitable security can make partners more willing to enter an agreement and help clarify responsibility for failure. A planned reserve can improve continuity. It may also reveal that a proposed commitment is unaffordable before the organisation accepts obligations extending beyond its initial funding.
NATURE-18.limitations: Guarantees may need collateral, premiums or cash held aside. Conditions and exclusions can leave gaps. A bank guarantee of payment does not prove ecological success, and a reserve cannot solve an unlimited restoration liability. Security requirements can make small projects disproportionately expensive.
NATURE-18.next_steps: Read the actual contractual requirement and identify the risk being secured. Compare guarantee costs, reserve funding and insurance with appropriate advice. Define measurable triggers and release conditions, and show restricted cash separately from spendable resources. Avoid counting the guarantee’s face value as project income.

NATURE-19.title: Green loans
NATURE-19.availability: Repayable funding subject to lender approval and use-of-proceeds conditions.
unresolved: What lender conditions and cash flow support repayment?
NATURE-19.what: A green loan finances investments meeting a lender’s environmental criteria. It remains debt, with repayment, interest and any reporting or security requirements set by the agreement. Concessionary terms may exist in particular products, but the green label alone does not establish a lower cost or public subsidy.
NATURE-19.fit: Illustrative fit: a paid restoration business finances suitable equipment, or a viable monitoring venture invests in delivery capacity. Algarrobos would need a credible source of repayment, not simply an expectation that improving habitat will eventually attract voluntary buyers or another grant.
NATURE-19.advantages: An appropriate product can align finance with environmental investment and allow a business to retain ownership. It may bridge the timing between spending and reliable revenue. Environmental criteria can also help structure evidence about how borrowed money is used and what the investment achieves.
NATURE-19.limitations: Interest, fees, covenants and repayment continue even if ecological outcomes or customer demand disappoint. Grant delays and drought can strain cash flow. Some green criteria may not fit the site’s ecological priorities. A loan for non-revenue conservation can create obligations the organisation has no means to meet.
NATURE-19.next_steps: Request the lender’s eligibility rules and complete written terms. Prepare cash-flow scenarios, including delayed receipts, and check the full cost and security. Compare the general loan node and any public participative loan separately; record a single borrowing transaction once, even if several labels apply.

NATURE-20.title: Ownership investment with conservation commitments
NATURE-20.availability: Requires a suitable ownership structure, investor and enforceable conservation terms.
unresolved: What legal ownership vehicle and exit restrictions protect conservation?
NATURE-20.what: An investor acquires an interest in a company or asset structure that includes conservation objectives. The investment can support operations or land management, but ownership rights, returns and exit remain central. Community ownership and commercial equity can involve very different legal and financial arrangements.
NATURE-20.fit: Illustrative fit: a viable company combines paid restoration services with protected conservation areas under clear governance. Another possibility is a collective ownership structure for a larger initiative. A small donation-funded association should not be described as selling dividend-bearing equity to its members.
NATURE-20.advantages: Shared ownership can mobilise capital and engage participants in long-term decisions. A carefully designed structure may align business income with conservation responsibilities. Investors can contribute management experience and networks, provided those benefits match the organisation’s actual needs and capacity.
NATURE-20.limitations: Returns, valuations, decision rights and exit expectations can conflict with ecological permanence. Asset sales or refinancing may weaken protection unless safeguards are enforceable. Legal setup and reporting can be expensive. An attractive conservation narrative does not establish that an investment is lawful, affordable or commercially viable.
NATURE-20.next_steps: Define the legal vehicle and who will own land, data and equipment. Assess revenues and obligations under conservative assumptions. Agree voting, transfers, exit and conservation protections with suitable advice. Compare impact equity and environmental funds as potentially overlapping descriptions rather than independent extra capital.

NATURE-21.title: Public fiscal mechanisms supporting conservation
NATURE-21.availability: A policy route requiring legal authority; no new local deduction or earmarked tax is assumed.
unresolved: Which existing law and competent authority permit the proposed fiscal mechanism?
NATURE-21.what: A public authority uses a lawful tax, incentive or allocation mechanism to direct resources toward conservation. The design can reward eligible behaviour or dedicate specified revenue. It depends on legislation and public administration, rather than a project deciding for itself that a conservation activity deserves tax relief.
NATURE-21.fit: Illustrative fit: a municipality and competent advisers examine whether an existing lawful incentive or budget arrangement can support stewardship. Algarrobos could contribute evidence of local needs and practical delivery costs. That is policy development, not an immediately available application for money.
NATURE-21.advantages: A durable public mechanism could support conservation beyond individual campaigns and link beneficiaries with public objectives. It may help normalise ongoing maintenance as a public responsibility. Researching existing powers can reveal practical options already available within an authority’s lawful framework.
NATURE-21.limitations: Authorities cannot invent arbitrary exemptions or levies outside their competence. Legislative change, public approval and administration can take considerable time. Distribution and fairness matter. A general suggestion in a financing study is not evidence that a specific mechanism exists or applies to a particular landowner.
NATURE-21.next_steps: Identify the competent authority and actual legal basis before proposing a financial amount. Ask how eligibility, collection, allocation and reporting would operate. Compare ordinary municipal budgets and existing charitable incentives first, and keep advocacy or feasibility work separate from funds that are legally committed.

NATURE-22.title: Green, social and sustainability bonds
NATURE-22.availability: Institutional debt financing requiring an issuer and repayment capacity; not a small-project grant.
unresolved: Which institutional issuer and eligible investment portfolio could include the project?
NATURE-22.what: A bond issuer borrows money from investors through a debt security. A green or sustainability framework specifies eligible uses or related commitments and reporting. Investors still expect repayment under the bond’s terms. A project might receive financing within a larger portfolio without itself issuing a bond.
NATURE-22.fit: Illustrative fit: a public authority or substantial organisation includes suitable nature-based infrastructure in an approved investment programme. Algarrobos might contribute a small delivery or monitoring component through a separate agreement. Issuing a bond directly for a small experimental parcel would generally be disproportionate.
NATURE-22.advantages: At an appropriate scale, bonds can mobilise substantial long-term capital and organise environmental reporting across a portfolio. An institutional issuer may coordinate investments that are too large for local appeals. The instrument can connect conservation-related assets with established financial planning.
NATURE-22.limitations: Issuance, disclosure, verification and administration are complex and costly. The issuer needs creditworthiness and repayment resources. A green designation is not evidence of a grant, guaranteed ecological additionality or accessible finance for any landholder. Debt obligations continue regardless of how successful the environmental narrative becomes.
NATURE-22.next_steps: Look for an actual issuer and eligible project pipeline rather than trying to invent a security for the pilot. Check the framework, use of proceeds, reporting and delivery arrangements. Compare simpler loans or participation in a public programme, and treat bond-related contracts as their own specific transactions.

NATURE-23.title: Lawful user charges
NATURE-23.availability: Requires the legal power or authorised service arrangement to charge; it is not an NGO-created tax.
unresolved: Who has legal charging authority, for which service and under what access conditions?
NATURE-23.what: An authorised body charges for use of a facility, service or resource under the applicable legal framework. Proceeds may support upkeep or conservation where permitted. A compulsory public charge differs from a voluntary donation, and a private admission price differs from a municipal tax or fee.
NATURE-23.fit: Illustrative fit: an authorised operator includes conservation-compatible maintenance in a lawful visitor-service budget. Algarrobos would first need an actual service, appropriate access rights and an identified charging authority. A sensitive rural habitat might be unsuitable for visitor-based revenue at all.
NATURE-23.advantages: Where a real service and user base exist, charges can connect use with ongoing management costs. Predictable arrangements may support maintenance beyond a grant period. A transparent explanation can help users understand the relationship between their payment and the service or site they use.
NATURE-23.limitations: Legal authority, accessibility, collection costs and public-access obligations can limit the option. Demand may be seasonal and charging can exclude people. An association cannot simply impose a public fee on neighbours or visitors. Revenue assumptions must account for staffing, insurance and the ecological cost of use.
NATURE-23.next_steps: Clarify the service and legal basis before discussing a tariff. Ask the competent authority about approval, exemptions, allocation and reporting. Check conservation and grant conditions. Compare a voluntary add-on or a properly priced educational activity when those arrangements match the actual relationship more accurately.

NATURE-24.title: Conservation funding from land-value uplift
NATURE-24.availability: A specialised public-policy mechanism; no rural parcel entitlement or collection authority is assumed.
unresolved: Does a lawful land-value capture mechanism actually apply to this place?
NATURE-24.what: Land-value capture directs part of an increase in property value associated with public planning or investment toward public purposes. It requires a lawful mechanism for valuation, collection and allocation. The idea is different from a voluntary neighbour contribution or selling land that has appreciated in value.
NATURE-24.fit: Illustrative fit: a public green-infrastructure programme examines whether a legally established urban planning arrangement can help finance shared improvements. Algarrobos might learn from the approach for a wider municipal partnership, but a small rural conservation pilot is unlikely to be its direct organising scale.
NATURE-24.advantages: At the right scale, it can connect beneficiaries of public investment with some of its costs. It may support public infrastructure without depending entirely on annual fundraising. The concept encourages attention to who gains from landscape and access improvements and how benefits could be shared.
NATURE-24.limitations: Valuation and attribution are contested, and land markets can move for unrelated reasons. Public powers and planning procedures are essential. Collection may be slow or politically difficult. The project cannot assume that an estimated rise in nearby property prices is money available for its restoration budget.
NATURE-24.next_steps: Identify an existing legal planning instrument and the authority responsible for it. Assess whether conservation is an eligible use and what approval is needed. Compare municipal budgeting and voluntary contributions before investing in specialist design, and keep speculative land-value changes outside confirmed funding totals.

NATURE-25.title: Business districts pooling improvement funds
NATURE-25.availability: Requires an actual business partnership and lawful governance or collection arrangement.
unresolved: Do the businesses share a real benefit and an authorised funding arrangement?
NATURE-25.what: A defined group of businesses pools contributions for shared improvements, potentially including planting, visitor amenities or green infrastructure. In some jurisdictions formal business improvement districts have specific powers. An international example does not establish that the same legal structure or compulsory levy exists locally.
NATURE-25.fit: Illustrative fit: businesses in a visitor area voluntarily support a shared landscape or public-learning activity that benefits the area. Algarrobos could investigate a partnership if the geographical and economic connection is genuine. A remote rural plot with no shared customer base may have little fit.
NATURE-25.advantages: Coordinated support can make several modest business contributions useful at a practical scale. Shared administration and a common objective may sustain activities that one business would not finance alone. Local collaboration can also provide communication channels and introductions to other public or community partners.
NATURE-25.limitations: Businesses need a reason to cooperate and agreement on contributions, benefits and decisions. Formal district powers require the appropriate law. Commercial priorities may conflict with ecological needs or equitable public access. This is not a general subsidy available to every conservation organisation or rural landowner.
NATURE-25.next_steps: Map likely business beneficiaries and begin with a voluntary conversation about shared needs. Verify the applicable governance and funding mechanisms with the authority concerned. Cost a modest joint activity and define reporting. Compare ordinary sponsorship or beneficiary contributions when those simpler arrangements reflect what participants actually want.

FIN-DONATIONS-INDIVIDUAL.title: One-off donations
FIN-DONATIONS-INDIVIDUAL.availability: Requires willing donors; no open grant or pledged income is implied.
unresolved: Which recipient will accept gifts and what restrictions will donors impose?
FIN-DONATIONS-INDIVIDUAL.what: Individuals give money to a conservation organisation or an agreed project without receiving an ownership stake or a commercial product. The recipient accepts responsibility for using the gift as promised. A donation can be unrestricted or limited to a particular purpose.
FIN-DONATIONS-INDIVIDUAL.fit: Illustrative fit: a supporter pays for baseline field surveys, replacement plant guards or an independent ecological review. Small gifts could cover practical costs that are awkward to place in a competitive grant, provided the receiving organisation can account for them.
FIN-DONATIONS-INDIVIDUAL.advantages: This can start locally, with a clear explanation of the site and a modest, costed request. It can build relationships before a larger campaign. An unrestricted gift gives more room to respond to drought, damaged equipment or an unexpected monitoring need.
FIN-DONATIONS-INDIVIDUAL.limitations: Fundraising takes time and receipts are uncertain. Restricted gifts cannot simply be redirected. Receiving donations does not automatically make an association eligible to issue tax-deductible receipts. Personal accounts, unclear ownership of purchased assets and exaggerated ecological promises can undermine trust.
FIN-DONATIONS-INDIVIDUAL.next_steps: Choose the receiving legal entity, write the specific purpose and publish a transparent budget. Confirm donor privacy, accounting and receipt requirements. Show how results and expenditure will be reported, and distinguish expressions of interest from money actually received.

FIN-CROWDFUND-DONATION.title: Donation crowdfunding
FIN-CROWDFUND-DONATION.availability: A fundraising method requiring a launched campaign and actual contributions.
unresolved: Which platform terms, fees and delivery budget make the campaign feasible?
FIN-CROWDFUND-DONATION.what: A public campaign gathers many donations around a defined conservation purpose, often through an online platform. The platform provides collection tools and visibility; it does not itself award the campaign target. Donations may be conditional on reaching a stated minimum.
FIN-CROWDFUND-DONATION.fit: Illustrative fit: fund a first year of habitat observations and a small set of clearly justified field measures, explaining what each budget item enables. Photographs, baseline maps and an achievable reporting schedule make an unfamiliar restoration initiative easier to understand.
FIN-CROWDFUND-DONATION.advantages: Crowdfunding can test public interest and recruit future volunteers or recurring supporters. It lets a geographically dispersed community participate. A bounded campaign is easier to explain than an indefinite appeal to finance every part of a developing organisation.
FIN-CROWDFUND-DONATION.limitations: A successful campaign usually needs its own audience, preparation and sustained communication. Platform fees, payment processing, refunds and tax treatment affect usable proceeds. A target is not secured funding. Planting pledges should include establishment and follow-up costs rather than promising outcomes beyond the project’s control.
FIN-CROWDFUND-DONATION.next_steps: Compare platform terms, confirm the recipient and decide what happens if the target is missed or exceeded. Prepare the full delivery budget and evidence behind public claims. Coordinate with the donation and membership nodes so the same money is counted only once.

FIN-CROWDFUND-REWARD.title: Reward crowdfunding and advance sales
FIN-CROWDFUND-REWARD.availability: Requires customers, deliverable rewards and lawful trading arrangements.
unresolved: Can each reward be delivered profitably and lawfully, including cancellations?
FIN-CROWDFUND-REWARD.what: Supporters pay in advance for a promised reward, experience or product. Unlike a pure donation, this creates a delivery obligation. Depending on the arrangement, it can resemble a sale, with costs and consumer obligations that need to be planned before launch.
FIN-CROWDFUND-REWARD.fit: Illustrative fit: pre-sell a carefully prepared dryland restoration workshop or a printed field guide. A productive farm might explore advance sales of a lawful crop, but only with realistic supply and an agreed response to poor harvests or drought.
FIN-CROWDFUND-REWARD.advantages: Advance purchases can demonstrate demand and provide working capital before delivery. The reward also gives supporters a tangible connection with the project. It may suit a small educational or commercial activity better than a competitive grant with a long decision period.
FIN-CROWDFUND-REWARD.limitations: Sales income is not the same as a charitable gift. Production, postage, venue, insurance and platform expenses can consume the margin. Delays and refunds create liabilities. Access-based rewards must respect land permissions, ecological sensitivity and any public-funding conditions on the site.
FIN-CROWDFUND-REWARD.next_steps: Cost each reward, including staff time, taxes, cancellations and fulfilment. Check the seller’s legal position and publish clear terms. Keep the trading budget separate from conservation donations, and use a small pilot to establish whether buyers value the proposed product.

FIN-MEMBERSHIP.title: Memberships and recurring supporters
FIN-MEMBERSHIP.availability: Requires an operating membership or supporter scheme; income depends on retention.
unresolved: Is this legal membership, recurring giving or a paid service?
FIN-MEMBERSHIP.what: People make regular contributions to sustain an organisation or a conservation purpose. Formal association membership can include participation and voting rights; a recurring supporter plan may be a different arrangement. Its terms should explain which relationship the contributor is entering.
FIN-MEMBERSHIP.fit: Illustrative fit: local residents and remote supporters contribute toward repeat monitoring visits, basic insurance and annual reporting. A member-supported association could maintain continuity between grants, with a yearly account of the work and opportunities to discuss the project.
FIN-MEMBERSHIP.advantages: Recurring contributions can be more predictable than isolated appeals and can finance less visible running costs. They also create a community with an interest in long-term stewardship, which matters when ecological learning and recovery extend beyond a single planting season.
FIN-MEMBERSHIP.limitations: People can cancel, and administration, communication and payment failures take work. Benefits and governance must be affordable and fair. Membership does not automatically qualify contributions for charitable deductions. Do not tie essential grant-funded public participation to paid membership where the programme requires open participation.
FIN-MEMBERSHIP.next_steps: Choose whether this is legal membership, recurring giving or a paid service. Define rights, annual costs, cancellation and data handling. Build a conservative retention budget and explain which commitments remain deliverable if contributions fall. Compare the overlapping digital-membership option before adding both to a plan.

FIN-FOUNDATION-GRANTS-PRIVATE.title: Private foundation grants
FIN-FOUNDATION-GRANTS-PRIVATE.availability: Depends on a foundation’s current priorities, invitation rules and application window.
unresolved: Which foundation currently accepts this recipient and project purpose?
FIN-FOUNDATION-GRANTS-PRIVATE.what: A philanthropic foundation awards support from its own resources for purposes such as biodiversity, community development, education or research. Each foundation decides its geographical focus, eligible recipients, application process and reporting requirements. Some accept proposals; others work only through invitations.
FIN-FOUNDATION-GRANTS-PRIVATE.fit: Illustrative fit: a nonprofit partner seeks support for a documented dryland habitat pilot, landowner engagement or a public monitoring programme. A concise proposal can connect local needs with the foundation’s stated mission, rather than assuming every environmental donor funds land purchase.
FIN-FOUNDATION-GRANTS-PRIVATE.advantages: Private philanthropy can support exploratory work, organisational development or neglected costs when the donor’s rules allow it. A well-matched foundation may contribute expertise and introductions as well as money. Multi-year support can help maintain observations through variable weather.
FIN-FOUNDATION-GRANTS-PRIVATE.limitations: Competition and relationship-building can be substantial. A foundation’s existence is not an accessible open call. Restrictions on overheads, land ownership, onward grants or commercial activity may matter. Donor priorities can change, and an award rarely solves permanent maintenance without a wider financial plan.
FIN-FOUNDATION-GRANTS-PRIVATE.next_steps: Identify foundations whose published mission and recent grants match the proposed work. Verify recipient eligibility and whether unsolicited approaches are accepted. Prepare a realistic budget, governance information, ecological baseline and reporting proposal; record any invitation or deadline separately from this general funding mechanism.

FIN-CORPORATE-GIFT.title: Corporate charitable contributions
FIN-CORPORATE-GIFT.availability: Requires a corporate donor and agreed charitable purpose; no company commitment is assumed.
unresolved: Does the donor expect charitable acknowledgement or commercial deliverables?
FIN-CORPORATE-GIFT.what: A company gives money, equipment or other resources for a public-benefit purpose. A genuine charitable contribution differs from buying advertising or ecological credits. The agreement should identify the recipient, restrictions and the acknowledgement the company may receive in return.
FIN-CORPORATE-GIFT.fit: Illustrative fit: an employer supports a nonprofit’s field monitoring equipment or a public education programme near its workforce. A local business could donate suitable tools, with the recipient deciding whether they are useful and affordable to maintain.
FIN-CORPORATE-GIFT.advantages: Business relationships can mobilise practical resources and introduce additional supporters. A contribution may be simpler to organise than a certified environmental transaction. An unrestricted donation can help the organisation fund coordination and reporting that are otherwise difficult to finance.
FIN-CORPORATE-GIFT.limitations: Donor reputation and influence require attention. Contributions must not buy misleading claims that operations have become environmentally harmless.
