Tax treatment depends on the actual arrangement and recipient status. Donated equipment may bring storage, safety, servicing or disposal costs rather than usable cash.
FIN-CORPORATE-GIFT.next_steps: Agree the purpose, permitted public wording, accounting and any restrictions before accepting support. Check the donor’s expectations and conflicts of interest. Keep a separate record of sponsorship or service deliverables so a commercial exchange is not described as a charitable donation in public reporting.

FIN-SPONSORSHIP.title: Corporate sponsorship
FIN-SPONSORSHIP.availability: Requires a negotiated sponsor agreement and clearly priced deliverables.
unresolved: What publicity is being purchased and is it compatible with other funding?
FIN-SPONSORSHIP.what: A business pays for an association with a project, event or communication activity. It may receive agreed visibility, reporting or other promotional benefits. This is a commercial relationship whose obligations differ from a donation without a substantial return to the donor.
FIN-SPONSORSHIP.fit: Illustrative fit: a company supports a public field day and receives a modest acknowledgement on event materials. Another possibility is a sponsored annual habitat report with explicit editorial independence. These examples require agreement on access, evidence and the scope of publicity.
FIN-SPONSORSHIP.advantages: The project can offer a clear package of deliverables and develop a repeat relationship. Sponsorship may fund communication, coordination and participation. It can suit businesses that want visible local engagement but do not need a tradable ecological certificate.
FIN-SPONSORSHIP.limitations: The organisation must deliver what it sells. Advertising, invoicing and tax treatment need checking. Sponsor influence can compromise independent reporting, and commercial promotion may conflict with a grant’s nonproductive purpose. Financial support must not be translated into unsupported biodiversity or carbon-offset claims.
FIN-SPONSORSHIP.next_steps: Define the audience, deliverables, price, cancellation terms and permitted claims. Check compatibility with existing grants and land-use agreements. Require approval of public statements and preserve the ability to report disappointing ecological results honestly. Compare charitable giving if the business seeks no commercial return.

FIN-CSR-SUPPLYCHAIN.title: Business supply-chain stewardship
FIN-CSR-SUPPLYCHAIN.availability: A negotiated business arrangement; a buyer and relevant environmental dependency must be established.
unresolved: What actual local dependency motivates the company’s contribution?
FIN-CSR-SUPPLYCHAIN.what: A company supports conservation because water, soils, biodiversity or landscape resilience matter to its operations or suppliers. Support may take the form of a donation, a management contract or a shared project. The legal arrangement determines what the payer actually receives.
FIN-CSR-SUPPLYCHAIN.fit: Illustrative fit: a local agricultural buyer helps finance erosion observations and agreed soil-protection measures on participating farms. A catchment-dependent business might support a scientifically grounded water-management collaboration where its local connection and the project’s contribution can be demonstrated.
FIN-CSR-SUPPLYCHAIN.advantages: The motivation can extend beyond short-term publicity because the business benefits from healthier natural systems. Practical knowledge and access to producers can strengthen the project. A negotiated contribution may avoid the cost of creating a tradable environmental unit.
FIN-CSR-SUPPLYCHAIN.limitations: A company’s sustainability policy is not a funding commitment. Claims need to distinguish contributions from compensation for damage. Supply-chain influence, exclusivity, data access and management obligations can be demanding. Local actions cannot automatically offset impacts elsewhere or guarantee measurable water gains.
FIN-CSR-SUPPLYCHAIN.next_steps: Identify the company’s actual dependency, the decision-maker and a credible local objective. Agree responsibilities, monitoring, payment terms and permitted claims. Check whether the proposal is best recorded as a donation, sponsorship or ecosystem-service contract, and avoid counting the same contribution under several nodes.

FIN-LAND-DONATION.title: Donated land and conservation bequests
FIN-LAND-DONATION.availability: Depends on an owner’s consent and a legally completed transfer; no liquid income is created.
unresolved: Are title, liabilities, transfer costs and long-term upkeep acceptable?
FIN-LAND-DONATION.what: An owner transfers land or another asset to an organisation, during life or through an inheritance arrangement. Conditions may require conservation or restrict later disposal. A land gift changes ownership and responsibilities; it is not simply another source of spendable project cash.
FIN-LAND-DONATION.fit: Illustrative fit: a willing owner gives a suitable parcel to an established conservation body able to maintain it. A carefully agreed bequest could support future stewardship, while recognising that the timing and legal completion are uncertain until the estate is resolved.
FIN-LAND-DONATION.advantages: A secure conservation asset can remove a major barrier to long-term management. The donor may value continuity more than an immediate sale. A suitable property can support education, monitoring and partnerships, especially when accompanied by resources for ongoing costs.
FIN-LAND-DONATION.limitations: Title, boundaries, access, encumbrances, contamination and outstanding obligations require investigation. Taxes and transaction costs vary. Restrictions may be incompatible with the recipient’s capacity or other grants. A valuable asset can still leave the organisation unable to pay insurance, maintenance or necessary professional advice.
FIN-LAND-DONATION.next_steps: Inspect the land and legal title before acceptance, calculate whole-life costs and agree conservation, disposal and succession terms. Confirm the recipient’s powers and the donor’s tax position with appropriate advisers. Consider a stewardship agreement or long-term use right when ownership transfer is unnecessary.

FIN-CUSTODY-NOCASH.title: Land stewardship agreements
FIN-CUSTODY-NOCASH.availability: Requires a willing landholder and an enforceable agreement; it may provide rights rather than money.
unresolved: Which enforceable rights and duration satisfy the intended activities?
FIN-CUSTODY-NOCASH.what: Custodia del territorio is a land-stewardship approach in which landholders and conservation organisations agree how to protect or manage a place. The owner can retain ownership. Agreements can provide access, management cooperation or other rights without creating a grant or a cash receipt.
FIN-CUSTODY-NOCASH.fit: Illustrative fit: a landowner allows Algarrobos and a nonprofit partner to monitor native vegetation, compare low-disturbance measures and publish results. The agreement could specify which areas may be entered and which interventions require separate consent, reflecting the ecological sensitivity of the site.
FIN-CUSTODY-NOCASH.advantages: It can make practical conservation possible before buying land. Local relationships and shared objectives may provide continuity, while an experienced organisation contributes technical and administrative support. The existing COASTRUST material gives a local stewardship example, with its own specific context.
FIN-CUSTODY-NOCASH.limitations: An informal promise may not cover grant commitments or changes of ownership. Access, maintenance, liability, public participation, data and termination need definition. Rights contributed without payment are not automatically eligible grant cofinancing, and the agreement does not override environmental or land-use permissions.
FIN-CUSTODY-NOCASH.next_steps: Clarify the conservation objective and the rights actually required. Prepare a written agreement with duration, responsibilities, consent procedures and exit terms. Ask prospective funders whether those rights satisfy their conditions. Record any separate management payment under the relevant contract rather than inventing income here.

FIN-LEASE-USUFRUCT.title: Long-term land-use rights
FIN-LEASE-USUFRUCT.availability: Requires a negotiated legal right and an affordable long-term management arrangement.
unresolved: Does the proposed agreement cover the entire management commitment?
FIN-LEASE-USUFRUCT.what: A lease, usufruct or other recognised agreement allows an organisation to use land without purchasing full ownership. The rights, duration and costs depend on the chosen instrument. This node concerns enabling access and control; it does not represent new money arriving in the project.
FIN-LEASE-USUFRUCT.fit: Illustrative fit: secure enough time on a suitable dryland parcel to maintain monitoring plots and fulfil a conservation project’s follow-up commitments. A limited access permission might suffice for observation, while earthworks or permanent installations require broader, clearly documented authority.
FIN-LEASE-USUFRUCT.advantages: This can reduce the initial capital needed to begin work and let an owner retain the property. A well-designed agreement can support continuity and clarify responsibilities. It may also make it possible to work across several parcels rather than concentrating resources on a purchase.
FIN-LEASE-USUFRUCT.limitations: Rent, registration, taxes and legal costs can be significant. A short or revocable agreement may fail a funder’s requirements. Ownership changes, early termination, restoration of the site and ownership of improvements must be considered. Access rights do not automatically include permission for commercial or public events.
FIN-LEASE-USUFRUCT.next_steps: Define intended activities and required commitment length before choosing the legal instrument. Verify title, boundaries, existing restrictions and assignment rights. Cost the full term and agree what happens to equipment, plants and data at termination. Compare stewardship cooperation where fewer rights would achieve the objective.

FIN-PUBLIC-LAND-USE.title: Access to municipal or other public land
FIN-PUBLIC-LAND-USE.availability: Requires an authorised public-body agreement and the applicable allocation procedure.
unresolved: Which public-property procedure and authority can authorise this use?
FIN-PUBLIC-LAND-USE.what: A municipality or another public owner may authorise compatible use of land through a legally appropriate arrangement. Conditions depend on the property’s legal status and the public purpose. Public land cannot be treated as freely available merely because a conservation proposal sounds beneficial.
FIN-PUBLIC-LAND-USE.fit: Illustrative fit: a municipality explores a small public learning and monitoring site where native habitat management serves local residents. The project could combine observations, carefully managed visits and published results, provided the public authority approves both the use and the responsibilities.
FIN-PUBLIC-LAND-USE.advantages: The arrangement can connect a pilot with local policy, schools and public participation. It may avoid a land purchase and support continuity through an institutional partner. Public objectives can also help explain why observations and maintenance benefit a wider community.
FIN-PUBLIC-LAND-USE.limitations: An allocation may require competition, a concession, fees or other formal decisions. Existing users and environmental protections matter. Maintenance, public access, insurance and asset ownership require agreement. An official’s interest in the idea is not a completed authorisation or a promise of financial support.
FIN-PUBLIC-LAND-USE.next_steps: Identify the legal owner and property classification, then ask the competent department which procedure applies. Present the public benefit, activities, duration, costs and responsibilities. Confirm any grant compatibility before committing expenditure, and retain the actual authorisation as evidence for later planning.

FIN-PROCUREMENT-WORKS.title: Public restoration works contracts
FIN-PROCUREMENT-WORKS.availability: Only a published tender or other lawful procurement creates an opportunity; past works are precedents.
unresolved: Which live notice and supplier qualifications match the team’s capacity?
FIN-PROCUREMENT-WORKS.what: A public authority purchases defined works, such as river rehabilitation, erosion control or habitat restoration. The winning contractor earns revenue by meeting the contract. This is a supplier relationship with delivery obligations, rather than a subsidy for improving the contractor’s own land.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-WORKS.fit: Illustrative fit: a suitably qualified business supplies a small package of restoration works or maintenance within a larger project. Local documents from Níjar and the Andarax show the kinds of specifications and oversight involved, without establishing that those past contracts remain available.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-WORKS.advantages: A contract can connect practical ecological work with a paying client and a defined scope. Published specifications provide useful information about expected quality, quantities, scheduling and reporting. Subcontracting may offer a narrower entry point than taking responsibility for an entire works programme.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-WORKS.limitations: Tender eligibility, experience, capacity, insurance, guarantees, health and safety and working capital can be substantial. Price competition and payment timing affect margins. Changes or poor establishment can create liabilities. A contract’s plant list is not proof of a generally recommended ecological design.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-WORKS.next_steps: Search the official procurement platform for a current notice, then read the administrative and technical conditions together. Check the submission deadline and required qualifications. Price labour, equipment, maintenance and risk realistically; decide whether to bid, partner or approach an existing contractor lawfully.

FIN-PROCUREMENT-ENGINEERING.title: Public planning, mapping and engineering services
FIN-PROCUREMENT-ENGINEERING.availability: Requires a current procurement opportunity and the qualifications specified by the buyer.
unresolved: Which tasks require statutory qualifications, insurance and technical signatures?
FIN-PROCUREMENT-ENGINEERING.what: A public client buys professional services such as field surveys, project design, environmental documentation, mapping or construction oversight. GIS means geographic information systems: tools for organising and analysing spatial data. The service provider is paid for accepted deliverables and professional responsibilities.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-ENGINEERING.fit: Illustrative fit: a technically capable Algarrobos business maps vegetation, organises monitoring data or supports a licensed consultant preparing a restoration plan. The Rambla del Aljibe design specification is a local example of commissioned technical work, rather than an available landowner grant.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-ENGINEERING.advantages: This route can turn engineering, software and field skills into revenue without owning the work site. Clearly bounded subcontracted tasks may be realistic for a small team. Specifications also reveal which evidence public restoration projects need and where the team could build useful competence.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-ENGINEERING.limitations: Statutory design and certification may require particular qualifications, signatures and professional insurance. A general mapping service does not authorise every engineering responsibility. Tender capacity, data quality, intellectual property, liability and deadlines must be priced. Work already promised to another funder cannot be invoiced twice.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-ENGINEERING.next_steps: Identify current notices and distinguish the lead designer’s responsibilities from supporting tasks. Review competence and insurance requirements, payment milestones and ownership of data. Prepare a small portfolio of relevant work and a realistic service proposal before treating potential contract value as project income.

FIN-PROCUREMENT-PLANTS.title: Native plant and seed supply contracts
FIN-PROCUREMENT-PLANTS.availability: Requires a live purchasing opportunity and a compliant nursery or supplier.
unresolved: Can the supplier meet provenance, health, stock and delivery specifications?
FIN-PROCUREMENT-PLANTS.what: A public buyer or restoration contractor pays for plants, seeds or other specified reproductive material. The supplier must meet requirements for species, origin, stock quality, health, quantity and delivery. Income comes from a sale, not from a grant for planting on the supplier’s own parcel.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-PLANTS.fit: Illustrative fit: an appropriately registered nursery supplies locally suitable native stock to a larger restoration project. The Níjar supply specification provides an existing example of contractual plant requirements. It should be read as a procurement precedent, not a universal species recommendation for Algarrobos.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-PLANTS.advantages: Purchasing specifications can make customer demand concrete and support production planning. A specialist supplier may offer provenance records, reliable stock and delivery capability that a general contractor needs. The activity can complement a real nursery business and practical restoration knowledge.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-PLANTS.limitations: Growing cycles, drought, losses, storage and transport can create substantial financial exposure. Provenance and phytosanitary requirements are not optional marketing claims. Substituting species or stock sizes may need written approval. Revenue must cover unsold stock and compliance costs as well as successful deliveries.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-PLANTS.next_steps: Read the exact live specification, confirm supplier registrations and check whether the required stock can be produced or obtained lawfully. Document seed origin and quality checks. Price delivery, rejection and replacement risks, and agree responsibilities before accepting orders or forecasting sales.

FIN-PROCUREMENT-STEWARDSHIP.title: Paid stewardship services
FIN-PROCUREMENT-STEWARDSHIP.availability: A specific commissioned service is required; COASTRUST is a precedent, not a perpetual grant.
unresolved: Which actual commissioning programme has budget and an eligible procurement route?
FIN-PROCUREMENT-STEWARDSHIP.what: An authority or institution contracts for activities supporting land stewardship: coordination, participation, habitat follow-up, maintenance or reporting. Payment is for an agreed service. The existence of a stewardship agreement alone does not mean somebody has budgeted to pay its manager.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-STEWARDSHIP.fit: Illustrative fit: a competent local team organises landowner meetings, maintains a monitoring schedule or produces public reports for a funded programme. The COASTRUST procurement concerning Parque Gunter Kunkel in Níjar shows that stewardship-related work can be purchased through a defined contract.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-STEWARDSHIP.advantages: This route values organisational and community skills alongside field competence. A smaller service package may be more accessible than a large civil-works contract. It can help an organisation develop practical experience and relationships while the commissioning programme remains responsible for its wider objectives.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-STEWARDSHIP.limitations: A live notice, lawful commissioning route and eligible provider are still needed. Tasks, evidence, public participation and deadlines can be demanding. The project must manage conflicts if it is both a grant partner and a supplier. An old tender’s budget or funding split cannot be copied into another plan.
FIN-PROCUREMENT-STEWARDSHIP.next_steps: Identify actual commissioning bodies and current notices, then check procurement, independence and qualification requirements. Define deliverables and staff time, price coordination and reporting, and verify access to the relevant land. Record conservation rights separately from any service fee to avoid confusing enabling support with income.

FIN-COMMERCIAL-RESTORATION.title: Private restoration and maintenance services
FIN-COMMERCIAL-RESTORATION.availability: Depends on paying customers and signed service contracts.
unresolved: Which paying customers accept a fully costed and clearly scoped service?
FIN-COMMERCIAL-RESTORATION.what: A business sells practical restoration, design support or maintenance to landowners, farms, conservation organisations or other clients. The buyer pays an agreed price for defined work. Any environmental obligation or grant held by the customer is separate from the supplier’s own business income.
FIN-COMMERCIAL-RESTORATION.fit: Illustrative fit: offer carefully scoped native planting maintenance, erosion observations or assisted-regeneration management for a client with suitable permissions. A small pilot could establish actual labour costs and customer demand before expanding into equipment-heavy works or taking responsibility for complex ecological outcomes.
FIN-COMMERCIAL-RESTORATION.advantages: Services can generate income from existing skills and solve a practical customer problem. Repeat maintenance contracts can extend beyond initial installation. Direct feedback helps refine methods, pricing and reporting, while satisfied customers may provide references for later public procurement or partnerships.
FIN-COMMERCIAL-RESTORATION.limitations: Demand, ecological competence, insurance, safety, licences and cash flow determine viability. Poorly specified outcomes can transfer drought or establishment risk to the provider. Low prices may conceal unpaid travel and follow-up work. Related-party purchases funded by grants require particular scrutiny and clear separation of costs.
FIN-COMMERCIAL-RESTORATION.next_steps: Interview prospective customers, define a narrow service and prepare a complete cost estimate. Specify access, permits, acceptance, maintenance and payment terms in writing. Test a small contract, document results honestly and keep this trading activity distinct from a nonprofit’s restricted conservation donations.

FIN-COMMERCIAL-DATA.title: Monitoring, mapping and environmental data services
FIN-COMMERCIAL-DATA.availability: Requires a customer who values the deliverable; software ownership alone creates no revenue.
unresolved: Which validated deliverable will customers pay for repeatedly?
FIN-COMMERCIAL-DATA.what: A provider sells field observations, maps, analysis, reporting or software that helps another organisation manage environmental work. Services may use remote sensing, meaning observations from satellites or aircraft, alongside ground measurements. A subscription is viable only when ongoing customer value justifies ongoing payment.
FIN-COMMERCIAL-DATA.fit: Illustrative fit: deliver repeatable photo-point records and vegetation maps for a restoration contractor, or organise a nonprofit’s monitoring and grant-reporting data. A narrowly defined service could combine software and field skills without claiming that every detected vegetation change proves successful restoration.
FIN-COMMERCIAL-DATA.advantages: This can connect the project’s technical learning with customers who already need evidence. Reusable tools and consistent methods may reduce delivery cost over time. Good data can support practical decisions and reporting without requiring Algarrobos to own every monitored parcel.
FIN-COMMERCIAL-DATA.limitations: Accuracy, scientific interpretation, land access, privacy, drone permissions, data ownership and long-term support all matter. A dashboard alone is not a validated measurement method. Subscription promises can create permanent maintenance obligations. Funding for innovative technology has different requirements from ordinary paid consultancy.
FIN-COMMERCIAL-DATA.next_steps: Find a buyer’s specific reporting problem and test a small paid deliverable. Define validation, uncertainty, update frequency, data rights and support. Price field visits as well as development. Separate commercial revenue from any research grant and avoid charging two sources for the same work.

FIN-REGENERATIVE-PRODUCTION.title: Income from lawful farm and forest products
FIN-REGENERATIVE-PRODUCTION.availability: Requires a productive business, lawful harvest and real buyers; young restoration sites may have no saleable yield.
unresolved: Are lawful yields and sales sufficient after drought and full operating costs?
FIN-REGENERATIVE-PRODUCTION.what: A farm, agroforestry operation or forest enterprise earns money by selling lawful products. Conservation-compatible production can contribute to stewardship costs, but the sale must stand on its own agricultural and commercial merits. A tree’s presence does not automatically create harvest income or a certified premium.
FIN-REGENERATIVE-PRODUCTION.fit: Illustrative fit: an established rain-fed farm evaluates a realistic crop market while protecting valuable nonproductive habitat. A nursery could sell suitable native stock. Algarrobos would need to distinguish productive areas and their business costs from areas managed primarily for ecological recovery.
FIN-REGENERATIVE-PRODUCTION.advantages: A viable product can provide repeat income and link management with local customers. It can create a reason to maintain productive land over time. Where appropriate, genuine farming may also connect with agricultural support, although those payments require their own eligibility checks.
FIN-REGENERATIVE-PRODUCTION.limitations: Drought, crop establishment time, uncertain yields, labour, processing and market access can outweigh sales. Harvest and land-use changes may be restricted. Certification has costs and does not guarantee buyers. Converting valuable shrubland merely to obtain a crop or subsidy can undermine the conservation purpose.
FIN-REGENERATIVE-PRODUCTION.next_steps: Confirm land classification, lawful production and likely customers. Build conservative yield, price and full-cost forecasts over several years, including failed seasons. Check registration, food or plant-health obligations and any grant compatibility before counting product income or choosing a productive planting design.

FIN-DEBT-LOAN.title: Loans and bridge finance
FIN-DEBT-LOAN.availability: Repayable finance requiring lender approval and credible repayment; not a grant.
unresolved: What repays the loan if expected receipts are late or reduced?
FIN-DEBT-LOAN.what: A lender provides money that must be repaid under agreed terms. Bridge finance covers a timing gap, such as expenditure before a confirmed reimbursement. A revolving facility allows repeated borrowing within limits. Interest, fees, security and repayment dates determine its real cost.
FIN-DEBT-LOAN.fit: Illustrative fit: an established restoration contractor finances equipment or an accepted customer invoice. A grant recipient might investigate a short reimbursement gap only after checking award conditions, payment uncertainty and its ability to repay even if a claim is delayed or reduced.
FIN-DEBT-LOAN.advantages: Debt can align spending with later receipts and preserve ownership when compared with equity investment. It may let a viable service business take an order it could not otherwise finance. A limited, well-costed facility can be more suitable than waiting for another competitive grant.
FIN-DEBT-LOAN.limitations: A loan does not repair an activity with no realistic income. Collateral, guarantees, variable interest and delayed grant payments can create serious exposure. Uncontracted carbon or biodiversity sales are uncertain repayment sources. Public participative loans, ordinary bank lending and grant advances have different conditions.
FIN-DEBT-LOAN.next_steps: Prepare a cash-flow forecast with delayed receipts and lower-income scenarios. Obtain written lender terms and check security, early repayment and total cost. Confirm any assignment of grant receipts is permitted. Record borrowed money separately from available own funds and from financial support that need not be repaid.

FIN-IMPACT-EQUITY.title: Investment in a conservation-related business
FIN-IMPACT-EQUITY.availability: Requires an investable legal vehicle and negotiated ownership terms; no investor is assumed.
unresolved: Which ownership, return and exit terms preserve the conservation commitments?
FIN-IMPACT-EQUITY.what: An investor contributes capital in exchange for an ownership interest in a company and expects a financial return. Impact investors also seek credible social or environmental results. Equity is different from a loan: voting, profit distribution, dilution and eventual sale of the investment become important.
FIN-IMPACT-EQUITY.fit: Illustrative fit: a commercial monitoring company or restoration service business seeks capital to serve a demonstrable market. The business might support Algarrobos activities through a clear arrangement, but investors would need evidence that the company can earn revenue beyond the founder’s own pilot site.
FIN-IMPACT-EQUITY.advantages: Equity can finance development before regular cash flow and bring useful business experience. It does not usually require scheduled loan repayments, although investor expectations remain substantial. A suitable investor may support expansion and longer-term product development where immediate operating cash is limited.
FIN-IMPACT-EQUITY.limitations: Ownership and influence are shared. Growth, exit and return expectations can conflict with permanent conservation commitments. Ordinary nonprofit association members do not hold dividend-bearing shares. Valuation, intellectual property, related-party transactions and the separation of charitable assets from a commercial company require careful treatment.
FIN-IMPACT-EQUITY.next_steps: Define the business, customers, capital need and proposed legal structure. Develop realistic financial and impact evidence, then negotiate governance, conservation protections and exit rights. Compare a loan or philanthropic support when those instruments better match the activity, and count overlapping investment descriptions only once.

FIN-LOCAL-HUMAN-CAPITAL.title: Volunteers, training and donated resources
FIN-LOCAL-HUMAN-CAPITAL.availability: Requires willing contributors and suitable arrangements; in-kind support is not automatically eligible match funding.
unresolved: Which tasks, supervision and contributions are actually available and eligible?
FIN-LOCAL-HUMAN-CAPITAL.what: People and institutions contribute time, expertise, materials or equipment instead of unrestricted money. Examples include supervised volunteers, university fieldwork, donated tools and a municipality’s staff time. These resources can make work possible, but their usefulness depends on competence, timing and actual project needs.
FIN-LOCAL-HUMAN-CAPITAL.fit: Illustrative fit: a university helps design repeat observations, while trained volunteers collect agreed field records under supervision. A local partner might lend equipment for a public workshop. Sensitive habitat work still needs permission and an appropriate method, regardless of whether labour is paid.
FIN-LOCAL-HUMAN-CAPITAL.advantages: Contributions can build local knowledge, participation and relationships while reducing specific purchases. Specialist advice can improve project quality more than a small cash gift. Structured involvement also offers learning opportunities and can create continuity when participants understand the long-term purpose.
FIN-LOCAL-HUMAN-CAPITAL.limitations: Supervision, insurance, safety, accessibility and data quality have costs. Volunteers must not simply replace work that legally constitutes employment. Donated plants need suitable provenance and health. A funder may exclude volunteer time or equipment values from eligible cofinancing, even when the contribution is useful.
FIN-LOCAL-HUMAN-CAPITAL.next_steps: List the tasks and skills required, appoint competent supervision and agree responsibilities with each partner. Confirm safety and volunteer arrangements, document actual contributions and ask funders how they may be recognised. Keep in-kind resources separate from cash available to pay invoices.

FIN-TAX-INCENTIVES.title: Tax incentives linked to conservation giving
FIN-TAX-INCENTIVES.availability: Depends on the applicable tax regime, recipient qualification and donor circumstances; no deduction is calculated.
unresolved: Do the recipient, donor and transaction qualify in the relevant tax year?
FIN-TAX-INCENTIVES.what: Tax rules can encourage giving or reduce the net cost of qualifying activities. They are not an independent grant paid to a restoration site. In Spain, Law 49/2002 sets a conditional regime for eligible nonprofit organisations and incentives for certain charitable contributions.
FIN-TAX-INCENTIVES.fit: Illustrative fit: Algarrobos works with an established qualifying organisation that receives donations for agreed conservation work and handles the required evidence. A donor may find giving more attractive when the recipient can lawfully provide the appropriate certificate, subject to the donor’s own position.
FIN-TAX-INCENTIVES.advantages: A properly organised recipient can make repeated fundraising more attractive and transparent. Clear documentation gives donors confidence about the nature of their contribution. Understanding the regime also helps distinguish charitable gifts, sponsorship, membership payments and commercial purchases, which may be treated differently.
FIN-TAX-INCENTIVES.limitations: Registering an association does not automatically qualify it for every charitable incentive. Entity status, compliance, donor residence, the nature of the gift and the tax year matter. A property transfer can bring other taxes and costs. Publicity benefits or services can change the character of a contribution.
FIN-TAX-INCENTIVES.next_steps: Confirm the recipient’s actual qualifying status and reporting capacity before advertising deductions. Check the current law and obtain advice for the proposed arrangement, especially for foreign donors or property gifts. Publish accurate receipt information and show gross contributions separately from any donor-side tax benefit.
